# Isidāsītherīgāthā (Thig 15.1)
**ID:** Thig 15.1
**Section:** Therīgāthā (thig)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-2
**Title (Pali):** Isidāsītherīgāthā

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Isidāsītherīgāthā* (Thig 15.1, Thi 400–447) is a biographical poem of over forty verses preserved in the *Therīgāthā* [Norman 1983; Covill et al. 2010; Collett 2014]. Unfolding as a dialogue in Pāṭaliputta between the senior nun Bodhī and Isidāsī, the poem relates Isidāsī's entry into the Saṅgha after she was repeatedly rejected by three successive husbands despite her exemplary humility and diligence as a wife [Young 2004; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Drawn to monastic life upon meeting the ascetic Jinadattā, she was ordained with her father's blessing and subsequently attained arhatship [Horner 1930; Gombrich 2009]. Through the three higher knowledges, Isidāsī traces the karmic origin of her marital distress to an earlier life as an adulterous man; as retribution, she suffered in hell before enduring sequential rebirths as a castrated monkey, a castrated goat, a castrated ox, an intersex person, and a maltreated co-wife, culminating in her final, liberated life [Appleton 2010; Appleton 2014; Norman 1983].
Scholars have noted the distinct literary and doctrinal characteristics of the composition. It uniquely supplies an elaborate autobiographical rebirth narrative in place of a separate *Apadāna* [Norman 1983; Collett 2014]. I. B. Horner and Richard Gombrich observed that Isidāsī's encounter with Jinadattā and her expressed aim of exhausting evil karma (*nijjarā*) exhibit notable Jain resonances [Horner 1930; Gombrich 2009]. While its geographical setting and polished narrative style led some scholars to consider the poem a later addition composed after the Buddha's demise, K. R. Norman observes that its composition in the archaic Āryā metre demonstrates that it cannot be very late [Norman 1983; Nyanaponika et al. 2003].
